questions.text: Why did your team pick a relational database over a NoSQL store for your last new service?
You chose to rewrite a module instead of refactoring it in place. Walk your manager through why.
Why did you build this feature yourselves instead of using a third-party library or service?
A new teammate asks why the team uses a monorepo. Explain the reasoning.
Why did you decide to ship behind a feature flag instead of waiting until the feature was complete?
Your tech lead asks why you picked a queue instead of synchronous calls between two services. Answer.
Why did you cut a planned feature from this release? Explain it to the product manager.
Explain why you chose to add a cache rather than optimize the slow query directly.
Your manager asks why your project slipped two weeks. Explain what happened and what you are doing about it.
Give today's stand-up update: what you finished yesterday, what you are doing today, and what is blocking you.
A migration you own is halfway done. Give a status update to the teams who depend on it.
You are blocked waiting on another team. Explain the situation to your manager and what you need.
Summarize the state of last night's production incident for people who were not on the call.
Your project is on track, but one risk could delay it. Give the update and name the risk.
Give a one-minute update on your quarter's goals: what is done, what is at risk, and what you are dropping.
The feature you launched last week has a bug reported by customers. Update your manager.
Explain how your team's deployment pipeline works to a new teammate on their first day.
A product manager asks what technical debt is and why it slows the team down. Explain it.
Explain what an API is to someone in sales who keeps hearing the word.
Explain the system you work on most to a designer who just joined the team.
Explain why some bugs only appear in production and not on your laptop.
A new teammate asks how code review works on your team. Explain the process and why it exists.
Explain what caching is and when it causes problems, to a non-engineer.
Explain the main trade-off in the design you are working on now to someone outside your team.
A product manager wants a feature by Friday that you think needs two weeks. Push back.
Your manager asks you to skip writing tests to hit a deadline. Push back.
A senior engineer proposes a design you think is too complex for the problem. Push back in the review.
Another team asks you to take on their on-call duty for a month. Decline and offer an alternative.
You are asked to join a fourth project while three are still in progress. Push back.
A stakeholder wants to add scope to a release that is already at risk. Say no and explain why.
Your team wants to adopt a new framework you think is not worth the migration cost. Make your case.
A teammate wants to merge a large change without review because it is urgent. Push back.
Give a teammate feedback on a pull request that works but is hard to read.
Introduce yourself and your role at the start of a meeting with a new team.
Summarize the decisions from a long design meeting for people who missed it.
Ask your manager for time to work on a project you care about. Make the case.
Describe a technical mistake you made, what you learned, and what you changed afterward.
Ask a busy senior engineer for help with a problem you have been stuck on for a day.
Tell your manager what went well and what did not in your last project.
A colleague's change broke your service. Raise it with them without blaming them.
